lessons.title: Ionophores and their effects on feed efficiency
lessons.body: Ionophores are feed additives that change the bacteria in the rumen to improve feed efficiency. They are not antibiotics for treating disease; they are used continuously at low doses. Common ionophores include monensin (Rumensin), lasalocid (Bovatec), and salinomycin. In Africa, monensin is the most widely available, often imported from South Africa, Europe, or China. For cattle, the typical inclusion rate is 20â30 grams per tonne of feed for monensin, providing about 200â300 mg per head per day. For steers on high-grain diets, this can improve feed conversion by 5â10% and reduce bloat. Ionophores work by favouring Gram-positive bacteria that produce propionate, a energy source, while suppressing Gram-negative bacteria that produce methane and ammonia. This shift means more energy from the same feed. For a 300 kg steer eating 8 kg of feed per day, a 7% improvement saves about 0.56 kg of feed daily. Over a 120-day finishing period, that's 67 kg of feed saved per animal. To use ionophores, buy a pre-mix (e.g., Rumensin 200) and mix thoroughly into the total mixed ration (TMR) using a feed mixer. Start with a low dose and build up over 5â7 days to avoid feed refusal. Never exceed 33 g/tonne for monensin, as toxicity can cause heart failure. Do not feed to horses or dogs. In Africa, where feed costs are high, ionophores are one of the cheapest tools to improve profitability. Always store in a dry place and use within 6 months. Check local regulations; in some countries, ionophores require a veterinary prescription.

lessons.title: Probiotics, prebiotics, and direct-fed microbials
lessons.body: Probiotics, prebiotics, and direct-fed microbials (DFMs) are natural additives that support gut health and digestion. Probiotics are live beneficial bacteria, such as Lactobacillus and Bacillus species. Prebiotics are non-digestible fibres that feed these good bacteria, like mannan-oligosaccharides (MOS) from yeast cell walls. DFMs are specific strains of live microbes, often yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or bacteria. In Africa, yeast culture (e.g., Yea-Sacc) is popular because it is stable in heat and improves fibre digestion. For cattle, typical inclusion rates are 10â20 g per head per day for yeast, or 5â10 g for bacterial DFMs. These additives help during stress periods: weaning, transport, or high-grain feeding. They reduce diarrhoea, improve feed intake, and increase weight gain by 3â5%. For example, a feedlot in Kenya using Saccharomyces cerevisiae at 15 g/head/day saw a 4% improvement in average daily gain (ADG) over 90 days. Probiotics are not drugs; they are sold as feed supplements. You can buy them as powders or pastes. Mix into the feed or top-dress. Store in a cool, dry place; heat above 40Â°C kills live yeast. Prebiotics like MOS are often included at 2â5 g/head/day. They bind harmful bacteria like E. coli and prevent them from attaching to the gut. For small-scale farmers, using fermented feeds like silage naturally provides some probiotics. But commercial DFMs give consistent results. Always check expiry dates and buy from reputable suppliers. In Africa, look for products registered by your national drug authority. These additives are safe and leave no residues, making them ideal for organic or export-oriented beef.

lessons.title: Buffers and neutralizers for high-grain diets
lessons.body: When cattle eat a lot of grain, the rumen becomes acidic, leading to acidosis, off-feed, and even death. Buffers and neutralizers help keep rumen pH stable. Common buffers are sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), magnesium oxide, and sodium sesquicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate is the most used: include 0.5â1% of the total dry matter (DM) in the diet. For a steer eating 10 kg DM, that's 50â100 g per day. Magnesium oxide is stronger; use 0.2â0.4% of DM (20â40 g/day). Buffers work by neutralizing excess acid and maintaining pH above 6.0. In high-grain finishing diets (70â90% grain), acidosis is a major risk. Symptoms include loose manure, reduced feed intake, and laminitis. In Africa, where maize and sorghum are common grains, buffers are essential. For example, in South African feedlots, sodium bicarbonate is routinely added at 0.8% of DM. To use, mix the buffer thoroughly into the TMR. Start with a lower level and increase as grain increases. Do not exceed 1.5% sodium bicarbonate, as it can cause alkalosis and reduce intake. Magnesium oxide is often used in combination with bicarbonate for better results. Another option is sodium bentonite, a clay that absorbs toxins and slows starch fermentation. Use 1â2% of DM. Buffers are cheap and effective. A 50 kg bag of sodium bicarbonate costs about $30 in many African countries, enough for 500â1000 head-days. Always provide free-choice salt and clean water. Monitor manure consistency and feed intake daily. If cattle are off-feed, reduce grain and increase forage. Buffers are not a substitute for proper step-up feeding; they are a safety net.

lessons.title: Enzymes and feed processing aids
lessons.body: Enzymes are proteins that break down feed components, making them easier to digest. In cattle, the most common feed enzymes are cellulases, xylanases, and amylases. Cellulases break down fibre (cellulose) into sugars, improving forage digestion. Xylanases break down hemicellulose, also in fibre. Amylases break down starch. For cattle, adding enzymes can improve feed efficiency by 2â5%, especially with low-quality forages. Typical inclusion rates: 0.5â2 kg per tonne of feed for a commercial enzyme blend. For example, a blend of cellulase and xylanase at 1 kg/tonne improved fibre digestibility by 10% in a trial with zebu cattle in Ethiopia. Enzymes are also used in silage making to speed up fermentation. For silage, apply an enzyme inoculant at 1â2 g per tonne of fresh forage. This reduces dry matter losses and improves preservation. In Africa, enzymes are often imported and can be expensive, but they pay off when using crop residues like maize stover or sorghum stover. To use, mix the enzyme powder with a small amount of feed, then blend into the TMR. Do not mix with hot ingredients; heat above 60Â°C destroys enzymes. Store in a cool, dry place. Another processing aid is propionic acid, used as a mould inhibitor in silage and high-moisture grain. Apply 0.5â1% of fresh weight. This allows you to store grain at higher moisture, reducing drying costs. For small-scale farmers, simple processing like chopping and soaking can also help, but commercial enzymes give consistent results. Always buy from a reputable supplier and check the label for activity units. Enzymes are safe and leave no residues.

lessons.title: Growth promotants and implants: regulations and use
lessons.body: Growth promotants are substances that increase weight gain and feed efficiency. They include hormonal implants (e.g., trenbolone acetate, estradiol) and beta-agonists (e.g., zilpaterol). In Africa, regulations vary widely. South Africa allows some implants under veterinary prescription, while Kenya and Nigeria have stricter rules. Always check with your national drug authority. Implants are small pellets placed under the skin of the ear. They release hormones slowly over 90â120 days. Common implants: Ralgro (zeranol) for suckling calves, and Revalor (trenbolone + estradiol) for finishing steers. Typical gain improvement: 8â15% in ADG and 5â10% in feed efficiency. For a 300 kg steer, that could mean an extra 0.2â0.3 kg gain per day. However, implants require proper training. Use a clean implant gun, disinfect the ear, and place the pellet in the middle third of the ear. Avoid crushing the pellet. Withdrawal periods: usually 0 days for implants, but check local rules. Beta-agonists like zilpaterol are not approved in many African countries due to food safety concerns. In the EU and some African markets, hormone-treated beef is banned. If you sell to export markets, avoid implants. For local markets, implants can be profitable. Cost: about $1â2 per implant, returning $10â20 in extra gain. Always keep records of implant dates and batch numbers. Do not implant breeding stock. Use only approved products from licensed veterinarians. In summary, growth promotants are powerful but regulated; use them legally and responsibly.

lessons.title: Flavors, binders, and pelleting aids
lessons.body: Flavors, binders, and pelleting aids improve feed acceptance, pellet quality, and handling. Flavors mask unpalatable ingredients like urea or high levels of by-products. Common flavors for cattle include molasses, anise, and citrus. Molasses is the most used in Africa: add 3â5% of the diet to improve taste and reduce dust. For a 10 kg feed, that's 300â500 g molasses. Synthetic flavors are used at 0.05â0.2% of the diet. They are especially useful when introducing new feeds or medications. Binders hold pellets together and prevent crumbling. Common binders: bentonite (1â2% of diet), lignin sulfonate (0.5â1%), and guar gum (0.1â0.3%). In Africa, bentonite is cheap and locally available. Pelleting aids reduce friction in the pellet mill and improve pellet durability. Examples: fats and oils (1â3% of diet), water (added as steam), and surfactants. For small-scale pelleting, adding 1% vegetable oil can increase pellet production by 10â20%. When making pellets, the feed must be ground fine (2â3 mm) and conditioned with steam to 80â85Â°C. Then it is pressed through a die. Without binders, pellets may have high fines, which cattle sort out. Use a pellet durability index (PDI) test: a good pellet should have PDI above 90%. In Africa, many feed mills use molasses both as a flavor and binder. For on-farm pelleting, a simple hammer mill and pellet press can work. Always add binders gradually and mix well. Store pellets in a dry place to prevent mould. These additives are not drugs; they are processing aids. They improve intake and reduce waste, saving money.

quiz.q: What is the typical inclusion rate of monensin for cattle?
quiz.explanation: Monensin is typically included at 20-30 grams per tonne of feed to provide 200-300 mg per head per day.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common ionophore used in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Monensin (Rumensin) is a widely used ionophore for improving feed efficiency in cattle.

quiz.q: How much can ionophores improve feed conversion in steers on high-grain diets?
quiz.explanation: Ionophores can improve feed conversion by 5-10% in steers on high-grain diets.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe inclusion rate for monensin in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Exceeding 33 g/tonne of monensin can cause toxicity, including heart failure.

quiz.q: Which animal should never be fed ionophores?
quiz.explanation: Ionophores are highly toxic to horses and can be fatal.

quiz.q: What is a common probiotic used in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Lactobacillus is a beneficial bacteria used as a probiotic in cattle feed.

quiz.q: What is the typical inclusion rate of yeast culture for cattle?
quiz.explanation: Yeast culture is typically fed at 10-20 grams per head per day to improve fibre digestion.

quiz.q: What is a prebiotic?
options: B) Non-digestible fibre that feeds good bacteria
quiz.explanation: Prebiotics are non-digestible fibres like MOS that stimulate the growth of beneficial bacteria.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a direct-fed microbial?
quiz.explanation: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) is a common direct-fed microbial used in cattle.

quiz.q: How much can probiotics improve average daily gain in feedlot cattle?
quiz.explanation: Probiotics typically improve average daily gain by 3-5% in feedlot cattle.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of buffers in high-grain diets?
quiz.explanation: Buffers like sodium bicarbonate neutralize excess acid and maintain rumen pH.

quiz.q: What is the typical inclusion rate of sodium bicarbonate in a high-grain diet?
quiz.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is typically included at 0.5-1% of total dry matter.

quiz.q: Which buffer is stronger and used at 0.2-0.4% of DM?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium oxide is a stronger buffer used at 0.2-0.4% of dry matter.

quiz.q: What is a sign of acidosis in cattle?
options: B) Loose manure and reduced feed intake
quiz.explanation: Acidosis causes loose manure, reduced feed intake, and laminitis.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended level of sodium bicarbonate in cattle diets?
quiz.explanation: Exceeding 1.5% sodium bicarbonate can cause alkalosis and reduce intake.

quiz.q: Which enzyme breaks down cellulose in feed?
quiz.explanation: Cellulase breaks down cellulose (fibre) into simpler sugars.

quiz.q: What is a typical inclusion rate for a commercial enzyme blend in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Enzyme blends are typically added at 0.5-2 kg per tonne of feed.

quiz.q: What temperature destroys enzymes?
quiz.explanation: Enzymes are denatured and destroyed at temperatures above 60Â°C.

quiz.q: What is propionic acid used for in feed?
quiz.explanation: Propionic acid is used as a mould inhibitor in silage and high-moisture grain.

quiz.q: What is a common growth promotant implant for finishing steers?
quiz.explanation: Revalor (trenbolone + estradiol) is a common implant for finishing steers.

quiz.q: How much can implants improve average daily gain?
quiz.explanation: Implants can improve average daily gain by 8-15% in cattle.

quiz.q: Where should an implant be placed in cattle?
options: A) Under the skin of the ear
quiz.explanation: Implants are placed under the skin of the ear, in the middle third.

quiz.q: Which of the following is banned in many African countries due to food safety concerns?
quiz.explanation: Zilpaterol, a beta-agonist, is not approved in many African countries.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for most implants?
quiz.explanation: Most implants have a zero-day withdrawal period, but check local regulations.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of flavors in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Flavors like molasses mask unpalatable ingredients and improve feed acceptance.

quiz.q: What is a common binder used in cattle pellets?
quiz.explanation: Bentonite is a clay used as a binder at 1-2% of the diet to improve pellet quality.

quiz.q: What is the typical inclusion rate of molasses as a flavor in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Molasses is typically added at 3-5% of the diet to improve taste and reduce dust.

quiz.q: What does PDI stand for in pellet quality?
quiz.explanation: PDI (Pellet Durability Index) measures how well pellets hold together; a good pellet has PDI above 90%.

quiz.q: What is a common pelleting aid that reduces friction in the pellet mill?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable oil (1-3% of diet) acts as a lubricant and improves pellet production.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a feed additive?
quiz.explanation: Maize silage is a forage feed, not a feed additive.
